title: She looked faithful on the outside.
paragraphs: She looked faithful on the outside.
That is what makes Martha dangerous to modern Christianity.

Not because she hated Jesus.
Not because she rejected truth.
Not because she was rebellious.
But because she was busy around Jesus while neglecting the presence of Jesus.
And most people never notice the difference until their soul becomes dry, irritated, exhausted, and spiritually numb.

You can sing worship songs while your heart is starving.
You can serve in ministry while secretly resenting everyone.
You can build an entire identity around helping others while neglecting the One you claim to serve.
God saw it.
You knew.
The story is hidden inside one small moment in Scripture, but the language underneath the text reveals something terrifying that English translations barely capture.
In Gospel of Luke 10:38–42, Jesus enters the house of two sisters: Martha and Mary.
Most sermons reduce the passage into a simple lesson about priorities.
But the original Greek exposes a spiritual war happening inside Martha’s mind.
The passage says:

“Now as they went on their way, Jesus entered a village. And a woman named Martha welcomed Him into her house. And she had a sister called Mary, who sat at the Lord’s feet and listened to His teaching.”
— Luke 10:38–39
Then suddenly the atmosphere shifts.

“But Martha was distracted with much serving.”
— Luke 10:40

The Greek word for “distracted” is:
περιεσπᾶτο (periespato)

This word means:
“to be dragged away,”
“to be pulled apart,”
“to be over-occupied to the point of internal division.”
Read that again.
Martha was not merely busy.
She was internally torn apart.
The root imagery carries the idea of something being pulled in multiple directions at once.

Her body was in the room with Jesus.
Her soul was somewhere else entirely.
That is the hidden battle.
And if we are honest, many believers are living there right now.

Constant movement.
Constant obligation.
Constant responsibility.
Constant noise.
But inwardly fragmented.
The enemy does not always need to pull you into open sin if he can simply keep you spiritually scattered.
Because scattered people stop listening.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
The text continues:

“Martha came up to Him and said, ‘Lord, do You not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her then to help me.’”
— Luke 10:40
Now the deeper issue surfaces.
Busyness had slowly distorted Martha’s perception of Jesus Himself.
Notice her accusation carefully.
“Do You not care?”
That sentence did not begin in the kitchen.
It began in her heart long before it came out of her mouth.

This is what unchecked anxiety eventually produces:
a false view of God.
The Greek word for “serve” here is διακονία (diakonia).
Ironically, it is the same root connected to ministry and service.

Meaning:
Martha’s problem was not sinful laziness.
Her problem was that legitimate service became spiritually disordered.
You can do holy things with an unhealthy soul.
You can build ministry while neglecting intimacy with Christ.
You can become so obsessed with serving God that you stop hearing God.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
Jesus never rebuked her hospitality.
He rebuked her anxiety.

“Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things.”
— Luke 10:41
The double naming matters.
“Martha, Martha…”
In Hebrew thought, repeating a name carried deep emotional weight.

It was not humiliation.
It was compassion mixed with urgency.

Like:
“Abraham, Abraham.”
“Samuel, Samuel.”
“Saul, Saul.”
Jesus was not attacking her.
He was trying to rescue her before her soul collapsed under the weight she was carrying.
The Greek word for “anxious” is μεριμνᾷς (merimnas).

It comes from the root μερίζω (merizo):
“to divide.”
Again the same theme appears.

Division.
Fragmentation.
Inner splitting.
Martha’s greatest battle was not external workload.
It was internal disintegration.
And then Jesus says something almost offensive to modern productivity culture:

“But one thing is necessary.”
— Luke 10:42
One thing.

Not fifty.
Not endless striving.
Not constant proving.
Not exhausting performance.
One thing.

In Greek:
ἑνὸς δέ ἐστιν χρεία
(henos de estin chreia)

Literally:
“there is need of one.”
Jesus cuts through the chaos of Martha’s soul with terrifying simplicity.

One thing actually mattered most in that moment:
His presence.
His voice.
His words.
Mary understood this.
The Scripture says she sat at Jesus’ feet.
That phrase was not casual language.
In Jewish culture, sitting at someone’s feet meant positioning yourself as a disciple under a rabbi’s authority and teaching.
Mary was choosing surrender over self-importance.
Stillness over performance.
Presence over pressure.
And Martha could not understand it because anxious people often resent peaceful people.
Especially when peace exposes their inner exhaustion.
God saw it.
You knew.
The modern church praises Martha constantly.

We celebrate burnout.
We applaud exhaustion.
We reward visible activity more than hidden communion with God.
But heaven is not impressed by frantic spiritual performance.
In Psalm 46:10, the Hebrew text says:

הַרְפּוּ וּדְעוּ כִּי־אָנֹכִי אֱלֹהִים
(Harpu u’deu ki anokhi Elohim)

Most English Bibles translate this:
“Be still, and know that I am God.”
But “harpu” means far more than physical stillness.

It carries the idea:
“let go,”
“release your grip,”
“stop striving.”
That changes everything.

Many believers are not resting in God.
They are clenching spiritually.

Trying harder.
Running faster.
Doing more.
Fixing everyone.
Carrying burdens God never assigned to them.
Meanwhile their intimacy with Christ slowly dies underneath religious activity.

Then resentment appears.
Then comparison.
Then emotional numbness.
Then hidden bitterness.
Then spiritual fatigue.
And eventually they ask the same question Martha asked:
“Lord, do You even care?”
But the issue was never His absence.
The issue was misplaced attention.
The Gospel does not invite you into endless spiritual performance.
It invites you into reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
In Gospel of Matthew 11:28, Jesus says:
“Come to Me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.”
The Greek word for “rest” is ἀναπαύσω (anapauso).

It means:
“to refresh,”
“to restore,”
“to give relief from weariness.”
Not temporary distraction.
Soul restoration.
That is what Martha truly needed.

Not more helpers.
Not better organization.
Not a faster schedule.
She needed her soul re-centered around Christ Himself.
And maybe you do too.
Because some people reading this are exhausted in ways nobody sees.

Still smiling.
Still serving.
Still posting Scripture.
Still helping everyone else.
But inwardly you are fragmented.

You pray without listening.
You worship without wonder.
You serve without joy.
You obey without intimacy.
And Jesus is still saying:
“One thing is necessary.”
Not because service is evil.
But because service without communion eventually becomes emptiness wearing religious clothing.
The enemy loves believers who are too busy to sit with Jesus.
Because eventually busyness can imitate faith while slowly replacing it.
That is why repentance matters.

Not merely from obvious sins…
but from self-driven striving that quietly pushes Christ Himself into the background.
The cross of Jesus Christ was never about creating exhausted religious workers.
It was about reconciling broken sinners to God through grace.
Through His death and resurrection, Jesus did what human effort never could.

He carried the burden.
He paid the debt.
He conquered sin and death.
Salvation is not earned by how much you accomplish for God.
It is received by faith in the finished work of Christ.
That changes how you serve.

Because now obedience flows from intimacy…
not insecurity.

From love…
not panic.

From surrender…
not exhaustion.
Some of you have been serving for years while secretly starving spiritually.
And tonight the Holy Spirit exposed it.
Say it plainly.
“Lord, I’ve been busy but distant.”
Let people know they are not alone in this battle.
Follow if you are done with surface-level religion and want deeper truth rooted in Scripture and centered on Jesus Christ.
